Front matter: title, abstract, keywords: A Latch-On-Resistant, False-Alarm-Gated Lead-Time Metric for Bearing Anomaly Detection — and What It Reveals About SCADA-Rate Logging Ansh Goyal1 1 Jaypee Institute of Information Technology, Noida, India anshgoyal500@gmail.com ABSTRACT Bearing anomaly detectors are usually scored by classiﬁcation accuracy, which ignores how early a warning arrives and at what false-alarm cost. We make lead time the primary evaluation object with a latch-on-resistant, false-alarm-gated metric: warning time counts only when the pre-onset false-alarm rate is within a budget τ , so a constant-on detector is provably invalid. With it we test whether a SCADA historian’s bin-averaged logging destroys lead time relative to decimation. Eleven detectors—four statistical process control (SPC) charts, Isolation Forest, three deep reconstruction autoencoders, a root-mean-square (RMS) trend baseline and two one-class models—run under a controlled sampling sweep on four inferential datasets: XJTU-SY (n = 10), FEMTO/PRONOSTIA (n = 6), University of Ferrara (n = 6) and NASA IMS (n = 3). On IMS the variance-sensitive charts shift positively (3σ +15.1 h) but inconsistently across runs; no test survives Holm correction (N = 44; 0 of 44). Against a pre-speciﬁed ±1 h margin, the resolution at which a planner can act, the difference is equivalent to zero in all 33 cells of the three multi-bearing campaigns, none favouring decimation beyond −0.45 h; IMS is too wide to decide in 9 of 11 cells and favours aggregation beyond the margin in 2. A single gas-turbine record of the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) cannot be tested. The powered campaigns are short-lived bearings, on which an IMS-sized effect could not appear, so the null bounds the effect at minutes, not hours. On these bearings deep models do not overtake the charts at any training fraction in [0.20, 0.60]; long-runway assets remain open. Code and results: https://github.com/ Ansh-Goyal01/Scada-Leadtime-Benchmark. Keywords: bearing anomaly detection, lead-time metric, false-alarm gating, SCADA historian, prognostic horizon, statistical process control, conformal prediction
Introduction: Condition-based maintenance (CBM) and prognostics and health management (PHM) replace ﬁxed-interval servicing with data-driven intervention, reducing both unplanned downtime and unnecessary maintenance (Jardine, Lin, & Banjevic, 2006; Lee et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2018). Rollingelement bearings are the most common failure mode in rotating machinery, and statistical control charts, classical machine learning and deep models are all used to detect incipient bearing faults from vibration (Randall & Antoni, 2011; Zhao et al., 2019). A warning delivered hours or days before a catastrophic seizure lets an operator schedule an orderly shutdown, order parts and avoid secondary damage to shafts, housings and couplings. Yet most published detectors are evaluated with classiﬁcation metrics—accuracy, precision/recall and receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC–AUC)—which answer “was the failure detected?” but not the planner’s question: “how many hours of warning did we get, and how often did the system cry wolf?” A detector that warns 48 h ahead at a low nuisance-alarm rate is operationally distinct from one that ﬁres minutes before breakdown or one that alarms every day. Time-aware prognostic metrics have long been advocated (Saxena et al., 2008; Saxena, Celaya, Saha, Saha, & Goebel, 2010; Goebel, Saha, & Saxena, 2011), yet lead time is rarely the headline quantity in detector benchmarks, and ad hoc deﬁnitions are easy to game: without a false-alarm constraint, a detector that alarms from the ﬁrst sample—a “latchon” exploit—earns the full run length as lead time while being operationally useless. A second question is practical. Industrial Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) historians rarely store raw high-rate vibration; they keep decimated or time-averaged summaries at a logging interval of seconds to minutes (Tautz-Weinert & Watson, 2017), not the tens of kilohertz at which accelerometers sample. The folklore concern is that bin-averaging these summaries washes out the excursions that signal an incipient spall, so that long-term storage would blind any prognostic algorithm that consumes the historian. To our knowledge this has not been tested with a sound lead-time metric across multiple datasets. If averaging is harmless, operators can store compact, cheap, bin-averaged streams without sacriﬁcing warning time; if it is harmful, prognostics-grade monitoring requires separate high-rate acquisition. We answer both questions. Lead time gated by a leakagefree pre-onset false-alarm rate is the primary metric, so the latch-on detector is provably scored invalid rather than winning. Under it we run a controlled sampling sweep that holds window content and alarm persistence constant, over nine headline detectors (four SPC charts, Isolation Forest, three deep reconstruction autoencoders and an RMS-trend baseline) plus two additionally evaluated one-class models, Deep SVDD (deep support vector data description) and a one-class SVM, on four inferential run-to-failure datasets—XJTU-SY (n = 10), FEMTO/PRONOSTIA (n = 6), University of Ferrara (n = 6) and NASA IMS (n = 3)—and a real single-asset ONGC gas-turbine SCADA record analyzed as a case study (Appendix D.2), with run-level signiﬁcance tests (the run, not the within-run sampling factor, is the unit of inference) and Holm correction. The folklore is refuted on every dataset tested: historian-style aggregation does not destroy lead time. The difference is negligible on the multi-bearing sets, positive but inconsistent in direction on IMS, and consistent with nondestruction on the turbine record. The defensible conclusion is bounded non-destruction: no dataset × detector cell shows decimation superior beyond a ±1 h operational margin, the resolution at which a planner can act (Section 6.4). Contributions. 1. A latch-on–resistant, false-alarm-gated, onset-relative lead-time metric, crediting warning time only when the false-alarm rate over a data-anchored, leakage-free pre-onset region is within a stated budget. A constant-on detector is provably invalid and one ﬁring just after the true onset is valid at zero false-alarm rate, by construction and by a released unit test. We do not claim the metric is unconditionally ungameable (Section 8). 2. A formal comparison showing that gating changes the answer, to our knowledge the ﬁrst: the ungated Saxena prognostic horizon (PH) makes a different and operationally misleading recommendation (Section 6.11). On IMS the seven detectors PH ranks highest—the deep models, the one-class SVM, Hotelling T 2, Isolation Forest and the exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) chart—have no valid operating point at a 10% budget; the gated metric picks 3σ, PH’s eighth. 3. A controlled SCADA-sampling methodology holding window content and alarm persistence constant, so an aggregate-vs-decimate difference reﬂects information loss rather than a window-counting artifact of coarser time grids. 4. A multi-dataset null result: with bootstrap conﬁdence intervals and run-level tests, SCADA-rate aggregation does not destroy lead time on any of the four inferential datasets, and nothing survives Holm correction across the N = 44 family. 5. Validation of a conformal detector for distribution-free false-alarm control; a lead-time–vs–false-alarm trade-off analysis; feature-group and spectral ablations that localize the prognostic signal to time-domain statistics on IMS; and deep reconstruction models (an LSTM autoencoder, a temporal convolutional network autoencoder (TCN-AE) and a transformer anomaly detector) that do not become competitive with SPC charts at training fractions in [0.20, 0.60] on short-lived bearings, a crossover on long-runway assets remaining open (Section 6.12). Scope of claims. The results are for rolling-element bearings under approximately steady operating conditions; we make no claim of transfer to gearboxes, blades or variablespeed machinery, and the sampling question is speciﬁcally bin-averaged versus decimated historian storage. The metric itself is failure-mode-agnostic: it applies wherever a run-tofailure trajectory and a stationary normal region exist. Our working hypothesis was that bin-averaging the stored summary series would wash out incipient-fault excursions and shorten lead time. It does not, and we report the refutation, with its dataset-dependent direction explicit, as more valuable than a tidy but unsupported positive claim.
Prognostics, CBM, and Lead-Time Metrics: Reviews of machinery diagnostics and prognostics (Jardine et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2018) and of remaininguseful-life (RUL) estimation (Si, Wang, Hu, & Zhou, 2011) establish the CBM/PHM framing in which a health indicator is tracked and an alarm or RUL estimate is produced. Saxena et al. (2008), Saxena et al. (2010) and Goebel et al. (2011) propose prognostic-performance metrics (prognostic horizon, α–λ accuracy, relative accuracy and timeliness) that reward early, well-calibrated predictions. Our onset-relative lead time is in this spirit: it measures warning time relative to a degradation event, not an arbitrary positional marker. We depart from prior practice by making the false-alarm budget part of the metric’s validity condition rather than a separately reported number, which closes the latch-on loophole, and we give what is to our knowledge the ﬁrst formal comparison showing that an ungated prognostic horizon ranks detectors differently, and misleadingly, from a false-alarmbudgeted metric (Section 6.11). The cost asymmetry between a missed detection and a false alarm has been treated explicitly outside bearing prognostics. The Numenta Anomaly Benchmark (Lavin & Ahmad, 2015) scores streaming detectors under an application proﬁle that rewards early detection and penalises false positives, making our gate’s commitment in another domain: earliness cannot be assessed independently of nuisance-alarm behaviour. The difference is structural. That benchmark folds both into one weighted score, so a detector may trade false alarms against earliness and still rank well; our budget is a validity condition, and an alarm outside it earns no credit that a longer lead can offset. A parallel line of work revises evaluation itself for time-series detection. Tatbul, Lee, Zdonik, Alam, and Gottschlich (2018) generalise precision and recall from points to ranges with a tunable positional bias, so early detection within an anomalous interval can be rewarded, and Wu and Keogh (2023) argue that widely used benchmarks admit trivial solutions and overstate progress. Our metric shares the diagnosis but reports a physical quantity—hours of warning—that a planner can act on, rather than a score on a bounded scale, and the false-alarm constraint gates validity rather than weighting the score.
Anomaly Detectors and Control Charts: Univariate and multivariate statistical-process-control charts—the 3σ rule, the exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) (Roberts, 1959) and Hotelling’s T 2 (Hotelling, 1947)—remain workhorses of industrial monitoring (Montgomery, 2009) because they are interpretable and need little training data. Isolation Forest (Liu, Ting, & Zhou, 2008) and the one-class support vector machine (SVM) (Schölkopf, Platt, Shawe-Taylor, Smola, & Williamson, 2001) are widely deployed unsupervised learners; LSTM autoencoders (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997; Malhotra et al., 2016; Hundman, Constantinou, Laporte, Colwell, & Soderstrom, 2018) and Deep SVDD (Ruff et al., 2018) have been applied to machine-health monitoring (Zhao et al., 2019). We evaluate both families under one ﬁxed hyperparameter protocol, so the comparison is about evaluation and sampling, not tuning. Relation to published FEMTO/XJTU results. The IEEE PHM 2012 challenge and later remaining-useful-life (RUL) studies on FEMTO/PRONOSTIA and XJTU-SY (Wang, Lei, Li, & Li, 2020; Nectoux et al., 2012) report a RUL-error score on deliberately truncated Test and Validation copies. It is not comparable to ours: they estimate a continuous RUL on runs with no observed failure and report no false-alarm rate, so their scores say nothing about whether an alarm would survive our τ gate, whereas we measure early-warning lead time on complete run-to-failure trajectories; tabulating one against the other would be a category error. The classic normalized-RMS health indicator with a ﬁrst-prediction-time threshold, the baseline underlying most of that literature, is our rms_trend detector; re-evaluating speciﬁc published architectures under the gated metric (which requires their original code) is future work. The pairing of detection delay with a false-alarm constraint is the founding formulation of sequential change detection. Lorden (1971) posed the minimax problem of minimising worst-case detection delay subject to a lower bound on the average run length to false alarm, Moustakides (1986) showed that the cumulative sum (CUSUM) chart of Page (1954) is exactly optimal under that criterion, and Pollak (1985) gives the corresponding result for a revised delay measure. Our gate inherits the premise but applies it when a detector is scored, against a rate measured on the data, rather than when it is designed by choosing a threshold that meets a run-length bound. The two can disagree: CUSUM has no valid operating point on IMS at a 10% budget, because its pre-onset false-alarm rate sits at 19.0–19.8% across every threshold we sweep. 2.3. Uncertainty Quantiﬁcation and Conformal Prediction
Uncertainty Quantification and Conformal: Conformal prediction (Vovk, Gammerman, & Shafer, 2005; Laxhammar & Falkman, 2014) bounds the false-alarm rate by a target α under exchangeability, converting a raw score into an alarm with an interpretable, ﬁnite-sample guarantee. We wire conformal calibration into the lead-time pipeline and test the guarantee empirically across runs, including a run where exchangeability provably fails because the “normal” region already contains degradation.
Vibration Features: Bearing-defect frequencies, spectral kurtosis (Antoni, 2006) and envelope (demodulation) analysis (Randall & Antoni, 2011) are the classical frequency-domain tools for bearing diagnostics. We include fast Fourier transform (FFT) band energies, spectral kurtosis and Hilbert-envelope amplitudes at the bearing characteristic frequencies, and ablate them against time-domain statistics to see which family carries prognostic lead time under the gated metric.
SCADA-Based Condition Monitoring: Tautz-Weinert and Watson (2017) review SCADA-data condition monitoring and note that historian aggregation is a recognized but under-quantiﬁed concern: practitioners suspect that coarse averaging hurts fault detection, but the effect has not been measured with a principled warning-time metric. We address this gap and ﬁnd that, for bearing faults, the concern is not borne out.
Datasets: We use four inferential run-to-failure datasets and a singleasset real-historian case study (Table 1), chosen so the sampling claim is tested under different conditions: a highrate raw-waveform rig where aggregation can be simulated faithfully (IMS), two multi-bearing campaigns (XJTU-SY and FEMTO/PRONOSTIA) that supply the statistical power a three-run rig cannot, a second modern constant-condition rig (Ferrara), and a historian stream that already is SCADArate data (ONGC, Appendix D.2). XJTU-SY (n = 10) is the primary inferential dataset; IMS (n = 3) is retained for its raw-waveform access, which permits the faithful aggregate/decimate simulation and the mechanism analysis (Appendix D.1). IMS. The NASA/IMS dataset (Qiu, Lee, Lin, & Yu, 2006) provides raw 20.48 kHz accelerometer waveforms for three run-to-failure tests on a shaft loaded with four bearings, so frequency-domain features (spectral kurtosis, envelope) are meaningful; the coarsening sweep itself acts on the windowed feature vectors, not the waveform (Section 4.8). The failure label of IMS test 3 is set as documented in the released repository and justiﬁed in Appendix C. XJTU-SY. The XJTU-SY dataset (Wang et al., 2020) contributes ten run-to-failure bearings under two operating conditions (ﬁve each) at 25.6 kHz, in 1.28 s snapshots once per minute. With n = 10 it gives the strongest generalization test here; its lifetimes range widely (52–533 min), stressing the metric with both long-degrading and abrupt-failure bearings. FEMTO/PRONOSTIA. The FEMTO/PRONOSTIA platform (Nectoux et al., 2012) contributes six Learning_set bearings under three operating conditions, with horizontal and vertical accelerometers sampled at 25.6 kHz in 0.1 s snapshots every 10 s. Only the Learning_set bearings run to the platform’s 20 g vibration stop, so a failure, and hence a lead time, is observed; the Test_set/Validation_set copies are truncated mid-life for the IEEE PHM 2012 RUL challenge and would leave lead time undeﬁned. Lifetimes span ∼1.4–7.8 h. We exclude the Paderborn dataset (Lessmeier, Kimotho, Zimmer, & Sextro, 2016): its pre-damaged bearings are measured at ﬁxed conditions for fault classiﬁcation, with no degradation timeline and no failure event, so it cannot test a lead-time or sampling claim, and using it would be a category error rather than a larger dataset count. University of Ferrara. The Ferrara dataset (Arpa, Gabrielli, & Battarra, 2024) contributes an independent 2024 campaign: six self-aligning double-row ball bearings under constant speed and radial load, with continuous uniaxial vibration at 25.6 kHz over each bearing’s entire lifecycle (ﬁve-second contiguous snapshots). Lifetimes span 0.7–6.8 h, similar to FEMTO. Fixed operating conditions make it directly compatible with our onset detector without normalization; we use all six runs (E1–E6), duplicating the single channel into the two channel slots so the channel-invariant schema applies unchanged. Like FEMTO and XJTU-SY, its short lifetimes mean it cannot conﬁrm or deny the IMS positive trend.
Problem Formulation and Notation: For each run we observe snapshots indexed by time t. A feature extractor maps each snapshot (and a short trailing window) to xt ∈ Rd; a detector assigns a score st and, through a threshold and a persistence ﬁlter, an alarm indicator at ∈ {0, 1}. Each run has a failure time tf and a train boundary tb, and all scaling and threshold statistics are ﬁt on {t ≤ tb} only. We measure the lead time (how long before tf the ﬁrst sustained alarm ﬁres) and the pre-onset false-alarm rate (how often the detector alarms while the machine is still healthy).
Channel-Invariant Feature Schema: Each snapshot yields per-channel time-domain statistics— RMS, kurtosis, skewness, peak-to-peak, crest factor and variance—and, for raw-waveform datasets, FFT band energies, spectral kurtosis (Antoni, 2006) and Hilbert-envelope amplitudes at the bearing characteristic frequencies (ball pass frequency outer race (BPFO), ball pass frequency inner race (BPFI), ball spin frequency (BSF) and fundamental train frequency (FTF)), computed from the dataset geometry. A naive scheme that concatenates per-channel statistics and all cross-channel pairs is channel-count dependent and illposed: it gives 445 features for a 4-channel run and 1465 for an 8-channel run against only ∼100 training snapshots (p ≫ n), so it overﬁts, silently inﬂates the apparent dimensionality and is not comparable across runs. We instead aggregate each statistic family across physical channels (mean and max) and summarize each aggregated series over a rolling window by its mean, standard deviation, maximum and lineartrend slope, plus one cross-channel RMS-coherence feature: a ﬁxed 49-dimensional space, identical for 4- and 8-channel assets and comparable across datasets (Appendix B). A trainﬁt variance top-k selection (k ≤ 50) then guarantees p < n, and all scaling is ﬁt on the training split only, so no test-region statistic leaks into the features.
Leakage-Free Degradation Onset: Lead-time metrics that reference an arbitrary positional marker (e.g. “the ﬁrst 5% of the test window is normal”) are gameable, because the marker is not tied to the physics of the run. We instead compute one degradation onset to per run from a scalar health indicator h(t), by default the element-wise maximum of the baseline-standardized mean- RMS and mean-kurtosis trends, so it responds to whichever degradation mode (amplitude growth or impulsiveness) appears ﬁrst: ( ) h(t) = max zb[RMS](t), zb[kurt](t) , (1) where the baseline mean µb and standard deviation σb of the z-score zb[·] are estimated only on data up to tb, so to cannot see the test region. With band β = µb + kσb (default k = 4), the onset is the start of the last sustained excursion above β before failure, to = min{ t ∈ Rlast : h(t) > β }, (2) where Rlast is the ﬁnal run of consecutive above-band samples, merging gaps shorter than a tolerance and requiring a minimum persistence (Algorithm 1). Using the last sustained excursion makes the onset robust to early run-in transients and to the single trailing machine-off sample, either of which could otherwise mark a spuriously early onset. Algorithm 1 Leakage-free terminal degradation onset The terminal-excursion rule has a predictable bias. For a degradation ramp of slope m the onset is late by approximately kσb/m, with a standard deviation of order σb/m. The persistence requirement P does not enter this bias: Algorithm 1 returns min Rlast, the start of the qualifying run, so P governs which excursions are admitted, not the timestamp reported for an admitted one. Bias and spread both scale inversely with the ramp slope: the estimator is near-unbiased and stable under abrupt degradation, where the delay falls to the sampling interval ∆t, and systematically late and more variable under gradual degradation. This accounts for Table 3, where the abrupt ﬁrst IMS test agrees across all three health indicators at 98–99% of span while the slow-degrading second and third tests move substantially. The persistence (5 samples) and gap (10 samples) tolerances are ﬁxed in samples of the health-indicator series, not physical time, and held constant across datasets, keeping the onset rule algorithmically identical everywhere at the price of physical-time comparability. At the native intervals (∼10 min per snapshot for IMS after resampling to a uniform grid, 1 min for XJTU-SY, 10 s for FEMTO and ONGC) the 5/10-sample bars correspond to ∼50/100 min on IMS, 5/10 min on XJTU and 50/100 s on FEMTO/ONGC. The difference is negligible for long records but not for the shortest bearings: XJTU Bearing2_4 (42 min total life) must clear a ∼5-minute persistence bar, roughly 12% of its lifetime. Caveat: onset positions on bearings with total lifetime below 2 h are treated as fragile throughout; per-bearing results in Tables 5 and 7 ﬂag these cases explicitly rather than silently discarding them. The sensitivity analyses probe the threshold multiplier k (Table 3), not these timing tolerances, which stay in sample units for algorithmic reproducibility.

If the pre-onset region is empty—the onset estimator places to at or before the ﬁrst scored window—FARpre is undeﬁned, the alarm cannot be gated, and it is excluded from the validity denominator rather than counted as valid. Why the metric defeats the latch-on exploit. A detector that ﬁres from the ﬁrst sample earns the full run length as L but ﬂoods the pre-onset region, giving FARpre ≈ 1 > τ , so the conjunction in Eq. (5) scores it invalid; a detector that ﬁrst ﬁres just after to has FARpre = 0 and L > 0 and scores valid. A unit test in the released code asserts exactly these two cases: a constant-on detector is invalid, and an oracle ﬁring at t+ is valid at zero pre-onset FAR. Because to uses only training-region statistics (Eq. 2), neither L nor FARpre can be tuned with test-region information. This defeats the speciﬁc latch-on exploit; it is not a claim of unconditional ungameability (Section 8).
Detectors: The headline set comprises nine detectors under one ﬁxed hyperparameter protocol: an RMS-trend naive baseline, which alarms when the mean RMS exceeds kσ above its training baseline and is included to verify that the metric penalizes a weak detector; the 3σ rule, alarming when the ℓ2-norm health index exceeds three training standard deviations; an EWMA chart (Roberts, 1959) (λ = 0.2, k = 3.0), sensitive to small sustained shifts; a deterministic two-sided tabular CUSUM chart (Page, 1954) (k = 0.5, h = 5.0) on the monitored magnitude, the classic change-point chart most sensitive to a small sustained mean shift such as slow degradation onset; Hotelling T 2 (Hotelling, 1947) in a principal component analysis (PCA)-reduced subspace (rank ≪ n), so the covariance is well-conditioned; Isolation Forest (Liu et al., 2008), an unsupervised ensemble that isolates anomalies with few random splits; and three deep reconstruction baselines—an LSTM autoencoder (Malhotra et al., 2016), a temporal convolutional network autoencoder (dilated causal convolutions) and a lightweight reconstruction Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017)—each trained on normal feature-window sequences only and scoring a window by its reconstruction error. Additionally evaluated. Two one-class models complete the eleven: Deep SVDD (Ruff et al., 2018), whose multi-layer perceptron (MLP) encoder maps normal data toward a ﬁxed center and scores a window by its squared distance to it, and the one-class SVM (Schölkopf et al., 2001). Deep SVDD is kept out of the headline set because it rarely alarms in time on short bearings (Section 6.12), but its numbers are reported in every result table because it is the low-false-alarm operating point under the gated metric (Section 6.9). The deep sequence models are data-starved: across bearings and training fractions the runs furnish between 20 and 335 normal training windows (median 88 at the default split). We include them as a modern-baseline comparison and to test whether a ﬁnite commissioning-data requirement makes them competitive with SPC charts (Section 6.12), without per-dataset tuning, the same ﬁxed-protocol fairness applied to the charts. A run with fewer feature windows than the sequence length (short XJTU bearings, some coarse IMS factors) cannot form a sequence; that (run, detector) cell is recorded as an explicit N/A, not dropped. All non-conformal detectors alarm via a percentile threshold on training scores followed by a persistence ﬁlter, so alarm semantics are identical across detectors and only the score differs.
Conformal Calibration: On IMS (Figure 4a, values in its caption) the distribution-free guarantee FAR ≤ α holds on test 2 (0% through α = 0.10) and on test 3 through α = 0.05 (0.9% at α = 0.01, 4.4% at 0.05), slightly exceeding the bound at α = 0.10, where the empirical FAR is 13%. It fails on test 1, at 0.74–0.85 regardless of α, for the reason Table 3 foretold: the onset ﬁres only ∼12 h before failure, so the “pre-onset” region already contains degradation and calibration and “normal” scores are not exchangeable. We keep this run because it delimits when the guarantee is usable in prognostics: it needs a genuinely stationary normal region, which an abrupt late-onset failure does not provide. On XJTU-SY (Figure 4b) bearings with a substantial stationary pre-onset region (e.g. Bearing2_3, calibrated through α = 0.05) honor the bound, while those with only one or two pre-onset windows, an artifact of short lifetimes, are ﬂagged uncalibrated rather than silently passed. The conformal machinery thus doubles as a per-asset usability test of whether enough stationary normal data exists to control the false-alarm rate at all. FEMTO and ONGC calibration. On FEMTO (Figure 4c) no bearing honors the bound at α = 0.05 (pre-onset FAR 0.08–0.56; pooled 0.27): the short 1.4–7.8 h lifetimes leave a pre-onset region that is neither long nor stationary. The most stationary bearings come closest (Bearing2_2 at 0.08, Bearing1_2 at 0.10) and the abrupt Bearing1_1 (0.56) violates it badly. On the real ONGC historian stream (Figure 4d) the calibration tracks the diagonal closely (empirical FAR 0.016, 0.030 and 0.096 at α = 0.01, 0.02, 0.05), a modest 1.5–2× above target, consistent with a mostly-stationary record that only mildly violates exchangeability. The guarantee is therefore usable where a stationary normal region exists (ONGC, the longer IMS/XJTU bearings) and self-reports as invalid where it does not (short FEMTO/XJTU bearings, abrupt onsets).
SCADA Sampling Sweep: We coarsen the time grid by a factor f ∈ {1, 2, 5, 10, 20} under two mechanisms: aggregate takes the mean within each bin of width f , exactly as a SCADA historian stores a bin-averaged value, and decimate keeps every f -th sample and discards the rest. A naive sweep changes the window’s wall-clock span as f grows, which alters lead time through a window-counting artifact rather than information loss. Our controlled sweep holds window content and alarm persistence constant so that only the effective logging interval varies, isolating whether averaging loses fault-relevant information relative to decimation.
At What Level Coarsening Is Applied: The aggregate and decimate operations are different experiments depending on the level at which they act, so we state that level for each dataset. On no dataset is the raw waveform coarsened: every loader reduces each snapshot to per-channel time-domain statistics at ingest, so the sweep operates on summary series throughout. On IMS the sweep coarsens the windowed feature vectors, after rolling-window summarisation, which holds window content and alarm persistence constant as the effective logging interval varies. On XJTU-SY, FEMTO/PRONOSTIA, University of Ferrara and ONGC the sweep coarsens the per-snapshot feature series: aggregate takes the mean of the summary statistics within each bin, and decimate retains every f -th snapshot. This is the operation a historian performs—historians store summary statistics, not waveforms—and it is the operation our claim concerns. It is not a test of raw-signal averaging. Averaging a raw waveform is a low-pass ﬁlter and does attenuate the impulsive transients that mark an incipient spall; we neither test nor dispute that, and Section 8 names it as the complementary study. The ONGC record is the clearest case, since its channels are the historian stream and no coarsening is simulated at all.
Statistical Protocol: Results are emitted in long format, one row per run × mode × factor × seed × method. Conﬁdence intervals bootstrap runs, the unit of generalization; resampling seeds would understate uncertainty. The run is the unit of inference. A physical bearing run produces one degradation trajectory; the ﬁve coarsening factors applied to it (f ∈ {1, 2, 5, 10, 20}) are repeated transformations of that trajectory, i.e. pseudoreplicates. Pooling them as 3 × 5 = 15 “pairs” per detector, as an earlier version of this work did, inﬂates the effective sample size ﬁvefold and yields overconﬁdent p-values. We therefore collapse each run to one difference, the mean of (aggregate − decimate) over factors: n = 3 on IMS, n = 10 on XJTU-SY, and n = 1 on ONGC, a single asset for which we report descriptive differences only. On these run-level differences we apply an exact two-sided sign test (binomial, H0 : P (aggregate > decimate) = 1 2 ), which uses only the direction of each difference and makes no normality or symmetry assumption that n = 3 could not support; a mixed-effects model with three random-effect lev- els would be over-ﬁt and is deliberately not used. The test cannot reach signiﬁcance at n = 3: all three runs concordant gives p = 2( 1 2 )3 = 0.25, so the IMS direction is a trend, not a signiﬁcant effect. Runs whose collapsed difference is exactly zero are excluded from the sign-test count, so the n+ and n− tallies count non-zero-difference runs only. Across the detector × dataset family (ONGC excluded) we control the family-wise error rate with the Holm–Bonferroni step-down procedure at α = 0.05, stating the family size N and the un- corrected FWER = 1 − (1 − α)N . One ﬁxed hyperparameter protocol avoids optimistic per-condition tuning.
Experimental Setup: All experiments use a ﬁxed random-seed protocol; stochastic detectors (Isolation Forest, the conformal wrapper) inject the seed explicitly, so runs are bit-reproducible. Extracted features are cached to Parquet so that the sweep, ablations, calibration and trade-off analyses consume identical features. The environment is pinned to the package versions that produced these numbers, and a 168-test suite asserts the metric’s ungameability properties, the leakage-free onset and the conformal factory. Every ﬁgure and table is generated from the released result tables; no number is hand-edited.

Sensitivity of the Onset Deﬁnition

Short-bearing onset stability. Over persistence ∈ {1, 3, 5, 10} windows (default 3; Table 4a) the median direction is stable but its run-level consistency is not: 3σ has one negative run at the default (n+/n− = 2/1, 3/0 elsewhere), EWMA is 2/1 at persistence 1, 3 and 5 and 3/0 only at 10, and Isolation Forest turns slightly negative at persistence 5. Aggregate vs Decimate on IMS: a Positive: Under aggregation, IMS lead time stays high and stable as the logging interval coarsens; under decimation it degrades faster, with 3σ and Isolation Forest collapsing at coarse intervals (3σ falls from 64.6 h at full rate to 24.8 h at 10× decimation while aggregation holds it near 64.6 h; Figure 3). The upturn at the largest factor is the few-windows regime, where only one or two runs survive and the mean is no longer comparable; we annotate rather than hide it. At the run level (Table 6) the magnitude-monitoring detectors show a positive median difference, the largest for 3σ (+15.1 h), but only CUSUM and Hotelling T 2 are sign-consistent: aggregation shortens the lead time of 3σ, EWMA and Isolation Forest on one run each, and Deep SVDD is positive in one run and tied in two. The three deep reconstruction models and the one-class SVM have negative medians, each with two negative runs and one positive, the deep models’ positive run being test 3; the RMS-trend baseline is mixed. With n = 3 the exact sign test cannot fall below p = 0.25, a ﬂoor only CUSUM and Hotelling T 2 reach, so nothing is signiﬁcant or survives Holm correction: the defensible reading is a null result with a positive median direction for the magnitude-monitoring detectors. The candidate mechanism is that bin-averaging acts as a low-pass ﬁlter suppressing single-window noise in the health statistic, so the alarm threshold is crossed earlier and held more persistently than under decimation; Appendix D.1 tests it and Section 7.3 gives the signal-theoretic reason.
Multiple-Comparison Correction: The aggregate-vs-decimate question is asked once per detector on each inferential dataset, a family of 11 × 4 = 44 tests (ONGC excluded) whose uncorrected family-wise error rate at α = 0.05 is 1 − (1 − 0.05)44 ≈ 0.90. Under Holm– Bonferroni no hypothesis survives (0 of 44): the smallest raw p is 0.125 (Transformer-AD on FEMTO), and every one of the forty-four adjusted p-values is 1.00. Lead-Time--vs--False-Alarm Trade-off: Sweeping the alarm-threshold percentile traces a prognostics analog of the ROC curve (Figure 5, Table 9): tightening the threshold lowers pre-onset FAR and lead together, so an operator can select an operating point for a stated false-alarm budget. On the achievable frontier Hotelling T 2 and Isolation Forest dominate the upper left, while the naive RMS-trend baseline collapses to near-zero lead once the threshold tightens (1.3 h at the 99.5th percentile). Hotelling T 2 has the highest raw lead of any control chart but exceeds the τ = 10% budget at every threshold tested, so it has no valid operating point on IMS; EWMA and CUSUM behave the same way, their pre-onset FAR sitting at 19.0–22.1% across the swept thresholds, so neither memory-based chart should be recommended under a 10% budget. Deep SVDD occupies the opposite corner, within budget (≤ 0.6% FAR) only by ﬁring late (≤ 14.8 h of lead). 3σ reaches a valid point, 56.3 h of lead at 8.9% FAR at the 99.5th percentile, and is the recommended chart under a 10% budget, a ranking that the raw-lead column of Table 2, led by the deep models, would by itself obscure. Feature-Group Ablation: On IMS, time-domain amplitude features (rms_only or time_only) give each of the six non-sequence detectors its highest or tied-highest validity, and adding spectral, envelope or all features never improves validity for any of them (Table 10). For the SPC charts the effect is sharp: rms_only is the unique group at which 3σ and EWMA reach full validity (1.00 at 0% pre-onset FAR), while spectral, envelope and all collapse all four charts to 0.33 by driving their pre-onset FAR to 42–63%, the variance-sensitive charts reacting violently to noisy extra dimensions. Deep SVDD fails the opposite way: its pre-onset FAR stays near 0% under every feature set, yet spectral features cut its validity to 0.33 (0.00 for spectral_only) by delaying or suppressing the alarm—missed detections, not false alarms. Under a false-alarm budget every detector should therefore be restricted to time-domain amplitude features, and frequency-domain features admitted with care, most of all for the SPC charts. Raw lead inverts this ranking without overturning it: on Isolation Forest the envelope group gives the longest mean lead (99.4 h) and rms_only the shortest (32.0 h), but the long-lead groups accrue 23–29% pre-onset FAR against 0.2% for rms_only, buying their lead by ﬁring indiscriminately; per run, spectral features ﬂip 3σ, EWMA and Hotelling T 2 from valid to invalid on test 2 at 100% pre-onset FAR while Isolation Forest stays valid in both settings. Repeated at every coarsening factor, rms_only stays uniquely best at native and 2× resolution (f ≤ 2), matching the argument that bin-averaging preserves the amplitude statistic; at f ≥ 5 only a handful of windows survive per run, valid fractions move in steps of 1/3, and whether the advantage holds at the coarsest SCADA rates is not resolvable at n = 3.
Comparison with the Saxena Prognostic Ho: If the false-alarm gate is what separates a usable warning from a manufactured one, a metric without it should reward detectors ours rejects. We test this against the most widely used ungated warning-time metric, the Saxena prognostic horizon (PH) (Saxena et al., 2008, 2010): PH = max(0, (tf − FAT)/3600) hours, with no false-alarm constraint. It is exactly our lead time L before the validity gate (Eq. 5) is applied, and that one missing conjunct is decisive. PH is maximized by the latch-on detector. On the three IMS runs the constant-on detector earns the full run length as PH (164–1073 h) while ﬂooding the pre-onset region (FARpre ≈ 1), so the gated metric scores it L = 0 on every run; the onset oracle is the mirror image, with zero pre-onset false alarms and the maximum achievable lead (12.9, 62.5 and 44.5 h). PH and L disagree on deployable detectors too. Ranked at their own best operating points (Table 2), the two orders nearly invert at the top. The seven detectors PH ranks highest—LSTM-AE 199.6 h, TCN-AE 185.4 h, Transformer-AD 184.0 h, the one-class SVM 180.2 h, Hotelling T 2 176.9 h, Isolation Forest 174.7 h and EWMA 89.1 h—have no valid operating point under a 10% falsealarm budget, so their gated lead is L = 0; the deep models alarm through 61–100% of every pre-onset region. 3σ, which PH ranks only eighth (77.0 h raw), is the one that clears the budget (56.3 h of lead at 8.9% pre-onset FAR) and the correct recommendation; CUSUM (65.0 h, PH’s ninth) also scores L = 0, and Deep SVDD, ranked last by PH, rises to a valid 14.8 h. Implication. Any warning-time metric that does not gate on FARpre can be driven to its maximum by loosening the alarm threshold, in the limit to the constant-on detector; ours closes this by construction and PH does not. On IMS this changes the recommended detector from the ones PH ranks ﬁrst by raw lead to 3σ, the only classical chart with a valid operating point at a 10% budget: PH rewards precisely the detectors a false-alarm-budgeted operator must avoid. 6.12. Minimum Training Data for Deep Anomaly
Minimum Training Data for Deep Anomaly D: How much normal run-in history must a new asset collect before a deep model can be trusted over a simple control chart? We sweep the training fraction T ∈ {0.20, . . . , 0.60} on FEMTO, the one dataset where all six bearings are long enough for every detector, including the seq-len-30 deep models (calibration ﬁxed at 0.10, test = 1 − T − 0.10, no per-T retuning). At T = 0.20 the shortest bearing (Bearing3_1) forms only 20 training windows, fewer than the 30 a sequence requires, so LSTM-AE, TCN-AE and Transformer-AD are explicit N/A there (Section 4.5); these are the only three N/A cells, the other 297 of the 300 (detector, bearing, T ) cells being genuine evaluations. Valid-alarm fractions use the full n = 6 with an N/A counted as no valid alarm, the conservative choice; the released sweep records the N/A count separately. There is no crossover (Figure 6). The four SPC charts are at or near their best at the smallest training fraction—3σ at 1.00, EWMA and Hotelling T 2 at 0.667, CUSUM at 0.500—and more commissioning data does not improve them: 3σ falls to 0.833 at T = 0.30 and 0.667 from T = 0.40 on, Hotelling T 2 falls to 0.500, EWMA is ﬂat at 0.667, and CUSUM is ﬂat at 0.500 apart from a one-bearing rise to 0.667 at T = 0.50. Isolation Forest starts and ends at 0.667 but dips to 0.167 at T = 0.30; only the naive RMS-trend baseline rises with T , from a far lower base (0.000 to 0.500). This is a consequence of the design, not reverse data-hunger: the test fraction 1 − T −0.10 shrinks as T grows, so on bearings this short a betterestimated baseline comes with a shorter window in which to use it. The three deep reconstruction models sit far below the charts at every training fraction (LSTM-AE and TransformerAD 0.000–0.333, TCN-AE 0.000–0.167) and do not close the gap. Deep SVDD has no valid alarm below T = 0.60 and 0.167, one bearing, at T = 0.60, the shortest test window: as on IMS test 1 it ﬁres very late, because its threshold requires substantial encoder-distance growth from the trained center, so on these 1.4–7.8 h bearings its ﬁrst alarm arrives at or after failure on all six bearings below T = 0.60 and on ﬁve of the six at T = 0.60. That is a bearing-lifetime constraint, not a training-data constraint. On bearings of the lifetimes tested here, control charts should therefore be preferred regardless of how much run-in history is available, because the deep reconstruction models do not overtake them anywhere in the [0.20, 0.60] training range. This is a statement about a data regime, not the architectures: across bearings and training fractions these runs furnish between 20 and 335 normal training windows, whereas the models carry 2.0–5.5×104 parameters, so the comparison is made where deep models are structurally disadvantaged. Whether a crossover appears on genuinely long-running assets, where a deep model could see orders of magnitude more normal windows, is the central open question (Section 8).
What Changed the Story: Four corrections, each described where it is applied, change the conclusion of an earlier version of this study: the corrected failure label of the third IMS test (Appendix C), the onset-gated metric that defeats the latch-on exploit (Eq. 5), the p < n channel-invariant feature space (Appendix B), and a signiﬁcance test on the run rather than the within-run sampling factor (Section 4.9). Together they turn the earlier claim that SCADA averaging destroys lead time into a refutation on every dataset tested, and the previously reported signiﬁcant positive effect into a non-signiﬁcant trend.
Why the IMS Trend Appears but Is Neutral: The IMS trend has a clean candidate mechanism (Section 7.3): bin-averaging is a low-pass ﬁlter that removes single-window noise spikes, so the variance-sensitive control charts (3σ, EWMA) cross and hold their thresholds earlier than under decimation, which keeps the spikes—consistent with the largest IMS median shift appearing for 3σ, though not with a consistent direction across the three runs. An ordinary moving-average or Kalman ﬁlter on the decimated stream reproduces the trend (Appendix D.1), so the mechanism is generic low-pass smoothing rather than historian averaging speciﬁcally. ONGC is already smoothed at the 10 s historian rate, so further aggregation adds little, and the short, often abruptly failing XJTU bearings leave little quiet runway over which averaging could help. The synthesis is therefore not “averaging helps” but bounded non-destruction: across very different regimes nothing favours decimation beyond the operational margin, and where the signal is noisy and the runway long, aggregation tends to stabilize the health statistic. The single-asset turbine case study. The one real historian record, an ONGC gas-turbine low-pressure-compressor bearing logged at a 10 s SCADA rate and ending in a genuine operator shutdown, is the cleanest illustration of the practical question because it needs no simulated coarsening: nine of its eleven detectors alarm 30–35 h ahead of the labeled failure (RMS-trend 22.8 h, and Deep SVDD not before failure at all), and the aggregate-vs-decimate difference is at most about a minute for every detector. As a single asset (n = 1) it supports no inference and is excluded from the inferential family (Appendix D.2).
Why Aggregation Preserves What Decimatio: Bin-averaging by a factor f is a length-f moving-average ﬁlter followed by downsampling: an anti-alias ﬁlter, then decimation. Plain decimation is the same downsampling with the ﬁlter omitted. The prognostic content of the health statistic evolves on the degradation timescale—hours—far below the post-coarsening Nyquist rate even at f = 20, while measurement noise in the same series is broadband. Decimation therefore folds out-of-band noise into the low-frequency band occupied by the degradation trend, raising the variance of the health statistic without changing its mean; aggregation attenuates that noise before downsampling. For a detector that alarms when the statistic crosses µb + kσb, a lower noise variance means the threshold is crossed earlier and held more persistently. The prediction that follows is about noise, not detectors: the advantage of aggregation should grow as the noise ﬂoor rises. It does, monotonically, from −0.35 h at the native noise level to +6.60 h at 10 dB, and an ordinary moving-average or Kalman ﬁlter on the decimated stream recovers it (Appendix D.1, Table 15). The feature space degrades unevenly under aggregation, for a structural reason. Each channel-aggregated series is summarised over the rolling window by its mean, standard deviation, maximum and linear-trend slope. The mean and the slope are linear functionals of the underlying series, so block-averaging them commutes with the summary up to the weighting induced by the 50% window overlap; the standard deviation, the maximum and the cross-channel coherence are not linear, and block-averaging them is not equivalent to computing the summary on the coarsened series. Aggregation therefore preserves the amplitude and trend descriptors more faithfully than the dispersion and extremal ones. We claim no conservation result. The detectors monitor a scalar collapse of the full standardised feature vector rather than any individual statistic, and the window overlap makes even the linear summaries a non-uniformly weighted average over each block. The argument states which descriptors degrade gracefully under aggregation and why the effect should track the noise ﬂoor; it does not predict the magnitude of the effect for any particular detector.
Practical Implications: For practitioners, storing bin-averaged vibration at SCADA rates, the default behavior of most historians, does not inherently sacriﬁce bearing-fault warning time relative to keeping decimated raw samples, and may improve it for control-chart detectors on noisy long-runway data. Conformal calibration adds a usable, distribution-free false-alarm guarantee wherever the normal region is genuinely stationary; the trade-off curve turns the gated metric into an operating-point selector for a stated budget; and the ablations caution that more features are not better under a false-alarm budget, time-domain amplitude and impulsiveness statistics carrying the usable signal on IMS. Where 3σ maximizes warning time within a 10% budget, operators whose cost structure penalizes false alarms heavily (for instance, process plants where each alarm triggers a mandatory manual inspection) have a complementary point in Deep SVDD, which stays within budget at ≤ 0.6% pre-onset FAR across the swept thresholds on IMS (Table 9) with 14.8 h of warning and near-zero false alarms. Neither should be used on IMS test 1, which the conformal machinery ﬂags as uncalibrated (Figure 4a).
Limitations and Threats to Validity: External validity (generalization). The IMS “aggregation helps” tendency is a non-signiﬁcant positive-median trend, sign-consistent only for CUSUM and Hotelling T 2 (n = 3), that does not replicate on the larger multi-bearing sets, so we claim only non-destruction as the cross-dataset headline, not a positive effect; ONGC (n = 1) is a descriptive case study with no inference. The datasets, while deliberately diverse, are all rolling-element bearings; we do not claim the result transfers to gearboxes, blades or other failure modes without further testing. A structural asymmetry limits what the cross-dataset null can establish. The three campaigns that supply statistical power—XJTU-SY, FEMTO/PRONOSTIA and University of Ferrara—comprise bearings whose total lifetimes span roughly 0.7 to 8.9 h, so an aggregation effect of the magnitude observed on IMS (a run-level median of +15.1 h for the 3σ chart) could not have been observed on them even if present. Their null therefore bounds the effect at the scale of minutes, which is what our equivalence margin reﬂects, not at the scale of the IMS result, while the only dataset whose runway is long enough to express such an effect has n = 3 and cannot reach signiﬁcance at any margin. We therefore claim non-destruction at short bearing lifetimes, where the evidence is strong, and consistency with—not demonstration of—non-destruction at the multi-week lifetimes typical of industrial assets. Residual gaming surfaces of the metric. We claim the metric defeats the speciﬁc latch-on (constant-on) exploit, not that it is unconditionally ungameable, and name two surfaces we do not close. (a) A detector could align its threshold to ﬁre just after to+; the onset uses only training-region statistics, so this cannot use test-region information, but an adversary who knows the onset rule could still tune toward it. (b) The onset health indicator shares its RMS/kurtosis basis with several detector features, so onset and detection are not fully independent, a circularity that could in principle favor detectors aligned to the onset statistic. Closing both (e.g. with an onset signal disjoint from the detector features) is future work. Construct validity (does the metric measure warning time?). The onset, although leakage-free and stable to k ∈ {3, 4, 5}, is not the ground-truth defect-initiation time, which is unobservable in these datasets. A late onset, as on IMS test 1 where degradation and failure nearly coincide, inﬂates the pre-onset region, can mark a genuine early detection invalid and breaks the conformal exchangeability assumption (Figure 4a). Bearings whose physics provides essentially no warning runway score zero valid alarms regardless of detector (Table 7), which is correct behavior but makes the valid-alarm fraction partly a property of the bearings, not only of the methods. Internal validity (is the comparison fair?). One ﬁxed hyperparameter protocol avoids optimistic per-condition tuning, the full trade-off sweep (Table 9) exposes threshold sensitivity rather than one hand-picked operating point, and the controlled sweep isolates information loss from window counting. Statistical-conclusion validity. Conﬁdence intervals are wide on IMS (n = 3); we resample runs, the unit of generaliza- tion, not seeds. An earlier pooled 15-pair Wilcoxon test treated the within-run factors as independent observations and thereby overstated signiﬁcance; the run-level exact sign test cannot fall below p = 0.25 at n = 3, and after Holm correction across the forty-four-test family nothing is signiﬁcant (Table 5), so the IMS result is a directional trend to be read with the multi-bearing nulls, never a signiﬁcant effect. The test itself sets the minimum dataset: signiﬁcance needs at least six sign-concordant runs (2( 1 2 )6 = 0.031), so the three IMS runs are at least a factor of two short—the quantitative content of the long-runway, many-bearing campaign that future work calls for. Such public datasets are rare; the closest single-bearing example is a KAIST bearing with a ∼43-hour lifecycle (n = 1, insufﬁcient for inference). Groups with long-running industrial historian archives (gas turbines, compressors, paper machines) can apply the released pipeline directly; loader templates for every public dataset format used here are included in the repository at https://github.com/Ansh-Goyal01/ Scada-Leadtime-Benchmark to minimize integration effort. Limited external benchmarking. We do not benchmark the gated lead-time metric against the RUL-estimation literature. The comparison is not straightforward—RUL methods predict a remaining-life quantity and are scored by prediction error, whereas our metric scores when an alarm ﬁres against a false-alarm budget—but the consequence is that the metric’s behaviour relative to that body of work is untested, and readers coming from RUL benchmarking should treat the two as complementary rather than ranked. Future work. Two extensions would sharpen these conclusions most directly: run-to-failure campaigns on long-life bearings typical of industrial service, whose multi-week runway could express an aggregation effect that short laboratory bearings cannot; and comparable work on other bearing types and geometries, since the four inferential datasets are all rolling-element bearings under approximately steady speed and load and the single real-asset record is one gas-turbine compressor bearing.
Conclusion: We presented a lead-time-centric evaluation protocol for bearing anomaly detection, whose onset-gated, false-alarmbudgeted metric defeats the latch-on exploit, and used it to test whether SCADA-rate logging destroys detection lead time. Across four inferential run-to-failure datasets (XJTU-SY n = 10, FEMTO/PRONOSTIA n = 6, University of Ferrara n = 6 and NASA IMS n = 3) and a real single-asset turbine SCADA case study (Appendix D.2), coarse aggregation does not destroy lead time; on IMS it shows a positive median shift for most control charts that is not consistent across the three runs, not signiﬁcant at n = 3 and not surviving multiple-comparison correction across the N = 44 family. No dataset × detector cell shows decimation superior beyond a ±1 h operational margin. That null is bounded by the scale of the evidence: the three campaigns supplying the statistical power comprise bearings of 0.7–8.9 h total life, on which an aggregation effect of the IMS magnitude could not have been observed, so the result bounds the effect at the scale of minutes and the multi-week runway remains untested. On the short-lived bearings tested, the deep reconstruction models do not overtake the control charts at any training fraction in [0.20, 0.60]; whether a crossover exists on long-runway assets is left open. The contribution is a reproducible methodology and a counterintuitive empirical result: non-destruction, not a guaranteed positive effect. Future work will learn the degradation onset jointly with the detector, so that the metric’s anchor no longer depends on a hand-set health indicator (closing the circularity noted in Section 8), and extend the conformal guarantee to the non-exchangeable early-degradation regime in which it currently fails. We release the full harness, detectors, tests, and the exact tables and ﬁgures of this paper to support replication and extension.

Appendix C: IMS Test-3 Relabeling Justif: An earlier label placed the failure of the third IMS test on 2004-04-08, leaving 21.5% of the recorded data after the nominal “failure”—impossible for a run-to-failure series. We relabel it to the last recorded sample (2004-04-18 02:42), at which the mean-RMS health indicator has ramped from its ﬂat baseline (∼0.068) to ∼0.228 before the ﬁnal machine-off reading: within the ﬂat normal-region baseline band at the old label, but well above the 4σ onset band at the corrected one. The relabeling moves the third test toward harder, not easier, detection: a run that was a guaranteed miss for most detectors becomes evaluable, and because the aggregate-vs-decimate contrast is computed within each run, the relabeling cannot artiﬁcially inﬂate it. It affects only the single hardest run and is not a tuning choice. We present it as an author relabeling based on the health-indicator trajectory, not independently veriﬁed ground truth: we know of no published benchmark that corrects this label, so we do not claim it as a community-established correction. It is the labeling we use throughout. The relabeling made our own claim harder to support, not easier. Because a reader may ask whether the label was chosen for the result it produces, we re-ran the entire IMS sweep under the original 2004-04-08 label and report both arms side by side (Table 14). The decisive case is 3σ: under the original label the third test is a guaranteed miss, both lead times are zero, the run’s collapsed difference is exactly 0.00 h, and the zero-difference rule of Section 4.9 leaves 3σ at two positive and zero negative runs. An earlier version of this work claimed that in no run does aggregation shorten the lead time of the magnitude-monitoring detectors. That claim would have been true under the original label; it is false only under the corrected one, where the third test contributes −1.00 h, and we have withdrawn it. The relabeling moved the evidence against the paper’s own claim rather than in its favor, the opposite of what a result-motivated relabeling would do. The relabeling is also narrower than one might expect. Under the original label the third test is a guaranteed miss for six of the ten detectors, not for all ten: 3σ, CUSUM, EWMA, Isolation Forest, Deep SVDD, and RMS-trend all score L = 0 in both modes. The remaining four—Hotelling T 2, LSTM-AE, TCN-AE, and Transformer-AD—alarm early enough to precede even the earlier failure time, so they retain a positive lead in both modes and their third run survives the zero-difference exclusion. The effective sample size is detector-dependent, and neither label can reach signiﬁcance. Because the zero-difference exclusion operates per detector, the original label does not simply reduce IMS to n = 2: it leaves neff = 3 for the four detectors that still warn on the third test, neff = 2 for 3σ, CUSUM, EWMA and Isolation Forest, and neff = 1 for Deep SVDD and RMS-trend. The exact two-sided sign test ﬂoors at p = 0.25, 0.50 and 1.00 at those sample sizes, so under the original label six of the ten detectors could not have reached α = 0.05 at any effect size, and the four with neff = 3 ﬂoor at p = 0.25, already above α. The corrected label retains every run, but n = 3 still bounds the attainable p at 0.25, so no IMS detector reaches signiﬁcance under either label and the best attainable p is 0.25 in both arms (Hotelling T 2). The label does not change the direction: no median ﬂips sign between the arms, 3σ holding at +15.10 h and Hotelling T 2 at +1.17 h, and the Holm verdict of Section 6 and the headline are untouched.
D.1 Generic Smoothing vs.\\ Historian Av: If bin-averaging helps on IMS because it is a low-pass ﬁlter suppressing single-window noise in the health statistic, letting the alarm threshold be crossed earlier and held more persistently than under decimation, two predictions follow. We test both on IMS at sampling factor 5, controlling window content so that only the smoothing differs. Prediction 1: the aggregate advantage should grow with noise. We add zero-mean Gaussian noise to the per-window health statistic at signal-to-noise ratios of 30, 20 and 10 dB and recompute the aggregate−decimate lead time, collapsing the four magnitude-monitoring SPC charts to one mean difference per run (n = 3 per level) to avoid the pseudoreplication corrected in the main analysis. The mean advantage rises monotonically with noise (Table 15a), from −0.35 h at the native noise level to +6.6 h at 10 dB, and at the two highest noise levels all three runs share the positive sign. The lone large negative, the −7.94 h native-noise entry, is IMS test 1, the abrupt near-coincident-onset run whose degradation begins only ∼12 h before failure, which also violates the conformal guarantee (Figure 4a) and is unwarnable under every feature set. This is the qualitative signature of a low-pass mechanism, the noisier the signal the more bin-averaging helps, but at n = 3 it is a directional trend, not a signiﬁcant effect (the exact sign test ﬂoors at p = 0.25, and at 30 dB the per-run signs are mixed): it corroborates the mechanism and cannot, at this sample size, establish it statistically. Prediction 2: any smoother on the decimated stream should recover the advantage. We compare a median ﬁlter, a moving average, a constant-velocity Kalman ﬁlter and a wavelet denoiser, each applied to the decimated stream, against raw aggregation and raw decimation (Table 15b). The moving average and Kalman ﬁlter recover essentially the full aggregate lead time (76.0 and 75.6 h vs. aggregation’s 75.6 h), while the median and wavelet ﬁlters fall slightly short, so the effect is generic smoothing of the health signal, not a property unique to historian bin-averaging: an operator who decimates and then lightly smooths recovers the same warning time. The wavelet denoiser drops to 6/12 valid alarms, below even raw decimation, because soft-thresholding the detail coefﬁcients perturbs the pre-onset baseline enough to lift the pre-onset false-alarm rate past the budget: smoothing that preserves the normal baseline recovers the lead time, while smoothing that distorts it can cost validity. The one-alarm gap between raw decimation (8/12) and aggregation (7/12) at statistically indistinguishable lead times (76.0 vs. 75.6 h) is sampling noise at n = 12, not evidence that decimation is preferable.
D.2 Single-Asset ONGC Case Study: The ONGC record is a real Solar-Turbine low-pressurecompressor (LPC) dataset: four vibration channels logged at a 10 s SCADA rate over ∼5 days (42,698 rows), ending in a genuine operator shutdown on 2023-11-13 09:46. This is authentic historian data with a real, documented event—the maintenance record conﬁrms the shutdown followed a rolling-element bearing fault on the LPC—and the data-derived degradation onset (2023-11-13 03:44) precedes the operator’s action by roughly six hours. ONGC is the only dataset that requires no simulated coarsening to be SCADA-rate: it is the historian. Nine of the eleven detectors alarm 30–35 h before the labeled failure (seven within 34.9–35.3 h, CUSUM at 33.9 h and Hotelling T 2 at 30.4 h), the naive RMS-trend baseline gives 22.8 h, and Deep SVDD does not alarm before failure. The aggregate-vs-decimate difference is at most about a minute for every detector (Table 6): on data that already is a real historian stream, the choice of logging mechanism does not materially change warning time, which is the cleanest possible illustration of the practical question and consistent with “averaging is not the enemy.” Because ONGC is a single asset (n = 1), we treat it as a descriptive case study and draw no statistical inference from it. Its conformal calibration (Figure 4d) tracks the diagonal closely, consistent with a mostly-stationary normal region.
